title: Applied anatomy: the anterior abdominal wall and laparoscopic port sites

guidelineVersions: Hurd et al., Am J Obstet Gynecol (1994)
Quint et al., J Laparoendosc Surg (1996)

related.why: The femoral triangle: the inferior epigastric artery again as the upper limit for femoral puncture

brief.scenario: Mrs Helen Marsh, 45, is having a diagnostic laparoscopy for chronic pelvic pain. She had an open appendicectomy as a teenager. The examiner will ask you about the anatomy of the anterior abdominal wall and read out the laparoscopic view.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the layers and blood supply of the anterior abdominal wall and on safe port placement.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Layers, sheath, vessels, then primary and secondary ports. The inferior epigastric artery links them.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Trusting transillumination to find the inferior epigastric artery. It shows only superficial vessels.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Skin, Camper's and Scarpa's fascia, three muscles, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, peritoneum."

grid.label: Layers
grid.fail: Misses transversalis fascia, or puts the muscles in the wrong order.
grid.pass: Skin, Camper's and Scarpa's fascia, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum.
grid.high: Adds that in the midline the layers fuse into the linea alba, which is why umbilical entry crosses few layers.

grid.label: Rectus sheath and arcuate line
grid.fail: Cannot say what changes below the arcuate line.
grid.pass: Below the arcuate line the posterior sheath is absent; rectus lies on transversalis fascia.
grid.high: The inferior epigastric vessels enter the sheath near the arcuate line, so a low lateral port meets them at the edge of rectus.

grid.label: Blood supply
grid.fail: Names only the superior epigastric artery, or gives the wrong origin for the inferior.
grid.pass: Superior epigastric (internal thoracic) and inferior epigastric (external iliac) anastomose in the rectus sheath. Superficial epigastric (femoral) runs in subcutaneous fat.
grid.high: Adds that the inferior epigastric vessels raise the lateral umbilical fold, seen at laparoscopy lateral to the medial umbilical fold.

grid.label: Primary port
grid.fail: Plans a blind Veress entry despite a previous laparotomy, or ignores the aorta.
grid.pass: Umbilical entry; the aorta bifurcates at L4, close beneath. After previous open surgery uses open (Hasson) entry or another site.
grid.high: Adds that in a thin patient the aorta lies close to the skin, and the umbilical position varies with body habitus.

grid.label: Secondary ports
grid.fail: Inserts lateral ports blind or through the rectus.
grid.pass: Inserts every secondary port under direct vision, lateral to the rectus edge, after seeing the inferior epigastric vessels.
grid.high: When landmarks cannot be seen, places lateral ports about 8 cm from the midline and at least 5 cm above the symphysis.

grid.label: Limits of transillumination
grid.fail: Relies on transillumination to avoid the inferior epigastric artery.
grid.pass: Transillumination shows superficial vessels only; the inferior epigastric artery must be seen laparoscopically.
grid.high: Adds that transillumination is less useful in obese patients.

grid.label: Recognising and controlling bleeding
grid.fail: Removes ports without looking, or does not know how to control bleeding.
grid.pass: Cannula and pneumoperitoneum can tamponade bleeding: inspects each site as the port is removed. Controls with pressure, diathermy or suture.
grid.high: Adds full-thickness suture or balloon tamponade, converting if uncontrolled; delayed rectus sheath haematoma can present after surgery.

fail.text: What are the layers of the abdominal wall?

fail.text: Skin, fat, the three muscles, then peritoneum.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What are the layers of the abdominal wall?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Skin, Camper's and Scarpa's fascia, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat and parietal peritoneum.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Below it the posterior rectus sheath is absent and rectus lies on transversalis fascia.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Superior epigastric from the internal thoracic and inferior epigastric from the external iliac, anastomosing in the sheath. Superficial epigastric from the femoral runs in the fat.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: At the umbilicus, but the aorta bifurcates at L4 just beneath, and she's had open surgery, so I'd use an open Hasson entry.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Under direct vision, lateral to the rectus, once I've seen the inferior epigastric vessels.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It only shows superficial vessels. I still need to see the inferior epigastric artery.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The port can hide bleeding, so I'd watch each site as it comes out, and control bleeding with pressure, diathermy or a suture.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Skin, Camper's and Scarpa's, the three muscles, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, peritoneum. In the midline they fuse as the linea alba, so umbilical entry crosses few layers.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The inferior epigastric vessels enter the sheath near the arcuate line, so a low lateral port meets them at the edge of rectus.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How do you find them at laparoscopy?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: They raise the lateral umbilical fold, lateral to the medial fold from the obliterated umbilical artery.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She is slim. Anything else at the umbilicus?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: In a thin patient the aorta is close to the skin, and the umbilicus moves with habitus, so I'd enter open.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: You can't see the vessels because of adhesions.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Then about 8 cm from the midline and at least 5 cm above the symphysis.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Transillumination is even less useful in heavier patients.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Full-thickness suture or balloon tamponade, converting if it won't stop. I'd also warn the ward about a delayed rectus sheath haematoma.

failures.consequence: The inferior epigastric artery is not seen, and a lateral port can transect it.

failures.move: Blind Veress entry after previous open surgery.
failures.consequence: Risks bowel adherent under the scar and, at the umbilicus, the aorta or iliac vessels.

failures.move: Removing ports without watching the sites.
failures.consequence: Bleeding tamponaded by the cannula is missed and presents later as haematoma.

failures.move: Inserting lateral ports blind or through the rectus.

recovery.when: You forget where the vessels run
recovery.line: The inferior epigastric vessels run up behind rectus, in the lateral umbilical fold.
I'd enter open, away from the scar, and place the rest under vision.

knowledge.fact: Below the arcuate line the posterior rectus sheath is absent.
Inferior epigastric artery: from the external iliac, behind rectus, in the lateral umbilical fold.
Without visible landmarks: lateral ports about 8 cm from midline, at least 5 cm above the symphysis.
Transillumination shows superficial vessels, not the inferior epigastric.

recall.think: Port-site injury: aorta at entry, inferior epigastric at lateral ports.
recall.say: "Open entry after previous surgery; lateral ports under vision."
do: Insert lateral ports lateral to rectus

numbers.meaning: lateral port from midline / above symphysis when landmarks unseen

recall.trap: Transillumination does not show the inferior epigastric artery.
recall.finish: Pressure, diathermy or full-thickness suture; convert if uncontrolled.

partner.opening: Mrs Marsh is on the table for laparoscopy. Name the layers of the anterior abdominal wall, from skin to peritoneum.

reveals.finding: Gridiron scar in the right iliac fossa; no other operations.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks what the laparoscope shows of the lower abdominal wall
reveals.finding: Read out: the laparoscope looks at the inside of the lower anterior abdominal wall. A single ridge of peritoneum runs in the midline from the dome of the bladder to the umbilicus. On each side of it, a second ridge runs from the pelvic side wall up to the umbilicus. Lateral to each of these, a lower, fainter ridge runs upwards and medially from just above the inguinal region and fades out below the umbilicus. On the left this outer ridge is clearly seen, with vessels running in it.
Blood runs down the left lateral port site as the cannula comes out.

push.question: What are the layers?
push.expect: Skin to peritoneum, including transversalis fascia.

push.question: What happens below the arcuate line?
In a transverse section of the abdominal wall midway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis, what lies directly behind the rectus muscle? How does that differ in a section above the umbilicus?
push.expect: Below the arcuate line: transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat and peritoneum, with no posterior sheath. Above it, the posterior rectus sheath lies behind the muscle.

push.question: Where does the inferior epigastric artery come from and run?
push.expect: External iliac; behind rectus; lateral umbilical fold.

push.question: How would you enter in this patient?
push.expect: Open entry; aorta bifurcates at L4.

push.question: Where would you place lateral ports?
push.expect: Under vision, lateral to rectus, after seeing the vessels.

push.question: On a diagram of the lower abdominal wall, a lateral port is marked at the lateral edge of the rectus, 3 cm above the pubic symphysis. Is that a safe site, and where would you move it?
push.expect: No: low and at the rectus edge, where the inferior epigastric vessels lie. Place it under vision lateral to the vessels; if they can't be seen, about 8 cm from the midline and at least 5 cm above the symphysis.

curveballs.prompt: The theatre light shows no vessels on transillumination. Is it safe to insert?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No. Transillumination misses the inferior epigastric artery; look from inside.

curveballs.prompt: On the ward she has a tender lower abdominal mass and falling haemoglobin.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Suspect rectus sheath haematoma from the inferior epigastric artery: resuscitate, CT angiography, senior review.

curveballs.prompt: Adhesions hide the lateral umbilical fold.
curveballs.safeAnswer: About 8 cm from the midline and at least 5 cm above the symphysis, under vision.
